fixes.explanation: True, baker. "Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived for fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel." (2 Kings 14:17). Jehoash is the king of Israel who beat him at Beth-shemesh. Amaziah was still around fifteen years after Jehoash was gone.

Not quite, friend. The text says Amaziah "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD…" (2 Kings 14:3). So the verse tells us he does what is right in the LORD's eyes. There's a catch coming in the same verse, but that first part is a good one.

That's it, baker. The text says Amaziah "…did everything as his father Joash had done." (2 Kings 14:3). Joash was the king before him. Amaziah is following Dad's example instead of King David's, and I can tell you it's easy to just keep doing what you watched somebody else do.

Right on the money, baker. The text says "…the people continued sacrificing and burning incense on the high places." (2 Kings 14:4). The high places were not taken away, so the people just kept right on doing it. Same habit, same spots.

That's right, baker. As soon as the kingdom was firmly in his grasp, "…Amaziah executed the servants who had murdered his father the king." (2 Kings 14:5). Joash was the king before him. I think this is a heavy part of the story.
Yes, baker. The command says, "Fathers must not be put to death for their children…" (2 Kings 14:6). A father isn't put to death for what his kids did. That's the first half of the rule.

Good one, baker. The command says, "…children must not be put to death for their fathers…" (2 Kings 14:6). A child isn't put to death for what a father did. That's the second half, and it's the command Amaziah follows when he doesn't put the murderers' sons to death.

That's the number, baker. "Amaziah struck down 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt." (2 Kings 14:7). That's a heavy part of the story, and the text gives the number plainly. He also took Sela in battle and called it Joktheel.

No wind in this story, friend. The text says, "…a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle." (2 Kings 14:9). Something with feet did the job. The thistle had asked for a cedar's daughter, and a beast came along.

No woodcutter here, friend. The text says, "…a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle." (2 Kings 14:9). It's a beast, and it trampled. The thistle is the one that sent the message asking for a marriage.
Not afraid, friend. Jehoash says, "You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud." (2 Kings 14:10). Proud is the word he picks. Those are his words about Amaziah.

Not weary, friend. Jehoash says, "You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud." (2 Kings 14:10). Those are his words, and proud is the one he chose. Weary doesn't show up in what he says.
No gift here, friend. Jehoash says, "Glory in that and stay at home." (2 Kings 14:10). He tells Amaziah to glory in his win and stay home. Nothing in the text about sending anything.
No truce here, friend. The text says "…Judah was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his home." (2 Kings 14:12). Judah lost and the men ran for home. A truce isn't in the story.

Amaziah lived through this one, friend. The text says "…Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah…" (2 Kings 14:13). He was captured, not killed. The text also says he lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash (2 Kings 14:17).

Yes, baker. Jehoash took "…all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace…" (2 Kings 14:14). Both places are named. That was a heavy loss for Judah.

Not the storerooms, friend. The text says Jehoash took the gold and silver "…found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace…" (2 Kings 14:14). Those are the two places named. The gates come up in the verse before, where Jehoash breaks down the wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate (2 Kings 14:13).

True, baker. Jehoash took "…some hostages. Then he returned to Samaria." (2 Kings 14:14). The hostages came along with the gold and silver. Then he headed back to Samaria, where he was later buried (2 Kings 14:16).

That's the place, baker. The text says Amaziah "…fled to Lachish." (2 Kings 14:19). He ran when the conspirators plotted against him in Jerusalem. Running didn't solve it, because men were sent after him to Lachish, and they killed him there.

That's him, baker. "…all the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah." (2 Kings 14:21). Sixteen years old and handed a kingdom. I think that's a lot to carry.

Close, friend, but not that one. Jeroboam was Jehoash's son and took over in Israel (2 Kings 14:16). In Judah, "…all the people of Judah took Azariah…" and made him king (2 Kings 14:21). Two kingdoms, two new kings.
